Gascony
GAS-ko-nee
n. (the south-western province of the Albret lands and the Gascon Huguenot nobility, and of Clairac and Nerac)
French Gascogne, from Vasconia, the land of the Vascones or Basques; the province lies between the Garonne and the Pyrenees.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Gascony is the south-western country whose nobility made the Huguenot cause a military power. A land of small towns, vineyards and a numerous and poor gentry with a strong tradition of arms, it fell largely within the Albret inheritance, so that when Jeanne d'Albret declared for the Reformation her Gascon vassals followed; Nerac became a Reformed court and Clairac, Caumont and a string of bastide towns held Reformed garrisons. Its Protestant gentlemen supplied much of the cavalry of the religious wars, and the king who ended those wars, Henry of Navarre, was raised among them at Nerac and Pau. That military character was the province's strength and its spiritual danger: a cause carried by gentlemen with horses and quarrels tends to be defended as a party and a privilege, and when Henry conformed to Rome in 1593 to secure Paris, a great part of the Gascon nobility followed him into the Catholic church within a generation, their estates being easier to keep that way. The dictionary enters Gascony because the Reformation there was genuinely held and largely held by a class, and when the class found its interest lay elsewhere the province went with it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a vassal as one who holds land of a superior; a bastide as a fortified town; cavalry as horsemen in military service; and to conform as to comply with or yield obedience.

expand to see more

VASSAL, n. A feudatory; a tenant; one who holds land of a superior and vows fidelity and homage to him.

FORTRESS, n. A fortified place; a large and permanent fortification for the defense of a country.

CAVALRY, n. A body of troops whose members serve on horseback; horsemen armed for war.

CONFORM, v. To comply with or yield obedience to; to make like in manners or opinions.

GENTRY, n. People of education and good breeding; the class between the nobility and the yeomanry.

Key Scripture

Mat 6:24 — "No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon."

Luk 18:23 — "And when he heard this, he was very sorrowful: for he was very rich."

Mat 19:22 — "But when the young man heard that saying, he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions."

1Ti 6:9 — "But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition."

Modern Corruption

South-western province of the Albret lands whose Huguenot nobility supplied the cause its cavalry, and largely followed Henry of Navarre back to Rome after 1593.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the religion held as a class interest, which is secure exactly as long as the interest runs with it. The Gascon gentry were Reformed because their overlords were and because the cause gave them standing, commands and a grievance against the crown; when the Edict of Nantes gave them security and the court gave their sons careers, the estates and the pensions argued the other way, and a great many conformed. The Lord's word is not a figure of speech: “No man can serve two masters” (Mat 6:24).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that property is the commonest obstacle to discipleship in Scripture's own examples. The young ruler “went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions” (Mat 19:22), and of the same man Luke records that “when he heard this, he was very sorrowful: for he was very rich” (Luk 18:23). The apostolic warning follows the Gascon pattern exactly, that “they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare” (1Ti 6:9). The dictionary records that many Gascon families did not conform and lost the estates instead.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek douleuo (G1398), to serve as a slave; Greek ktema (G2933), a possession; Greek pagis (G3803), a snare.

expand to see more

Greek douleuo (G1398) — to serve as a bondman; “No man can serve two masters”, Matthew 6:24.

Greek mammon (G3126) — riches, wealth personified; “Ye cannot serve God and mammon”, Matthew 6:24.

Greek ktema (G2933) — a possession, an estate; “for he had great possessions”, Matthew 19:22.

Greek perilupos (G4036) — very sorrowful, deeply grieved; “he was very sorrowful: for he was very rich”, Luke 18:23.

Greek pagis (G3803) — a trap, a snare; “fall into temptation and a snare”, 1 Timothy 6:9.

Usage

"“No man can serve two masters” (Mat 6:24) — a Reformed gentry whose interest changed after 1593."

"“for he had great possessions” (Mat 19:22) — estates easier to keep in the Catholic church."

"“they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare” (1Ti 6:9) — Nerac a Reformed court and Clairac a garrison."
